drafts.neutral_framing: Should Garland County government fund community food-growing programs, connecting and expanding the gardens, farmers market, gleaning and school programs already in the county?
drafts.final_wording: Should Garland County government fund community food-growing programs, connecting and expanding the gardens, farmers market, gleaning and school programs already in the county?
drafts.final_wording_note: Wording made neutral in October 2026; earlier wording is in the repository history.
shaping_notes: This is a policy question a county or city body could act on — not a named-individual conduct question and not an active ballot measure. It clears the charter’s bright lines.

A county cannot guarantee anyone’s food, and this question does not claim it can. Garland already has an active Master Gardener chapter, two existing community and school gardens, a year-round SNAP/WIC farmers market, and a regional food bank; the question asks whether the county should connect and expand them.
The sources are cited on the /food page. The food-insecurity figure differs slightly by data year (19.6% for 2022 vs. ~20% for 2023), and both are shown.
drafts.tier_note: Open as a Tier 0 sentiment poll during the site’s quiet launch: no account, one voice per browser, changeable until close. Per the charter, Tier 0 is displayed but never cited as verified resident opinion — verification tiers arrive with the full voting layer.
drafts.background: About one in five people in Garland County are food insecure — Feeding America’s 2023 estimate is ~20% (Aspire Arkansas), and the CHI St. Vincent 2025 Community Health Needs Assessment cites the 2022 figure at 19.6%, with the child rate at 26.2%. Most food assistance is emergency assistance. This question asks whether the county should also support growing and sharing food together. Garland has an active Master Gardener chapter, a year-round SNAP/WIC farmers market, existing school and community gardens, and a regional food bank moving 100,000+ lbs a month. Sources and precedents are on the Food as a utility page.
drafts.disclosure: This question was opened by the platform’s founder. It is disclosed because the platform names who opens every question.

drafts.final_wording: Should Hot Springs Utilities run a pilot of a biological filter before treatment?
drafts.final_wording_note: Framed as a pilot the utility can run on its own, measured before and after — not a commitment to build.
shaping_notes: A question about how our shared water is treated — not about any person, candidate, or ballot measure. Clears the bright lines.
Grounded in the utility’s own water-quality report and in published measurements of living filters, with their limits stated on the water page.
drafts.tier_note: Open as a Tier 0 sentiment poll: no account, one voice per browser, changeable until close. Tier 0 is displayed but never cited as verified resident opinion — verification tiers arrive with the full voting layer.
drafts.background: Hot Springs’ 2025 water report lists trihalomethanes at a highest running average of 74 ppb against an 80 ppb limit, with single readings up to 104 ppb. The limit applies to the running annual average. A biological filter is one method for reducing organic matter before chlorine is added; results vary by site. The evidence and its limits are on the water page.

drafts.background: The Garland County Detention Center is a University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture farm site that donates produce to Project Hope Food Bank (Garland County). Garland County Habitat for Humanity has built 170 homes in the Hot Springs area since 1995 (Habitat). A RAND meta-analysis of correctional-education studies found 43% lower odds of returning to prison among participants (RAND RR266). The facts, the evidence, and the limits are on the From holding to building page.
